messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh, a 76-year-old South Asian electrician, was mugged six months ago while leaving a late-afternoon job at a residential renovation. The sun was already low, casting long shadows across the empty street, when a man emerged from behind a parked van. He smelled strongly of alcohol—stale and sharp—as he shoved Rajesh against the brick wall, demanded his wallet, and yanked it from his back pocket before disappearing into an alley. Rajesh was not physically injured, but the suddenness of the grab, the reek of liquor in his face, and the helplessness of being pinned stayed with him. That night he woke from his first nightmare: the shove, the smell, the darkness of the alley, his own heart pounding. He lay in bed for hours, certain someone was outside.

In the weeks that followed, this sense of threat crystallized around specific triggers. Waking from a nightmare—which happened two or three times a week—left Rajesh disoriented and hyperalert; for the rest of the night, every creak of the house or distant car door felt like another approach. He began sleeping with the bedroom light on, his wife’s presence no longer enough to calm him. Crowded places became unbearable. At the hardware store, a line at the register or a cluster of shoppers near the power tools sent his shoulders rigid; he found himself scanning faces, checking exits, and sometimes abandoning his cart to walk out. The smell of alcohol—even a whiff from a stranger on the sidewalk—flooded his chest with that same helpless freeze he felt against the wall. Each of these triggers drove a sharp spike in threat monitoring: he grew vigilant not just at night but in daylight too, feeling threatened by strangers who approached him even to ask for directions or the time. A sudden movement beside him—a child darting past or a worker raising an arm to wave—made him flinch and brace.

His work as an electrician, once a source of pride, became a minefield. He used to take emergency calls at all hours, but now he refused any job after dusk, telling his boss he had “health issues.” On daytime jobs, he avoided basements and alleys, and he would not work alone if the house was empty. When a customer’s son ran up to him from behind on a job site, Rajesh spun around so fast he nearly dropped his voltage tester. The boy’s mother laughed it off, but Rajesh knew his reaction was not normal. He started leaving job sites early, claiming he felt dizzy. At home, he would not walk the dog after dinner, and his wife began taking over the grocery shopping because he complained that the aisles were too crowded.

The cycle became self-reinforcing. A nightmare left him exhausted and on edge, so the next day a crowded bus stop felt like an ambush waiting to happen. That feeling made him watch the crowd so intently that he spotted anyone who moved abruptly, which confirmed that his vigilance was necessary. Over months, Rajesh’s world shrank. He stopped attending the monthly electricians’ union meetings because the hall was always packed. He avoided the park where he used to walk, because too many strangers crossed his path. His wife noticed he no longer greeted neighbors; he once crossed the street to avoid a man who smelled of beer.

What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was an incident at a medical appointment. While waiting in a crowded clinic lobby, a man with alcohol on his breath sat down two seats away. Rajesh felt his chest tighten, his palms go cold, and before he knew it he had stood up, walked out, and sat shaking on a bench for twenty minutes. His wife, who had been inside, found him there and insisted he talk to someone. Now, sitting in the therapist’s office, Rajesh is quiet at first, then admits he is terrified that the mugging will happen again—that he will be caught off guard, that he will not be able to protect himself. More than anything, he wants to sleep through the night and walk into a store without scanning every face. He hopes, quietly, that talking will loosen the grip of that strange, rehearsed sense of danger that has taken over his days.
